exam.title: Linear Algebra - Intermediate Exam
exam.subtitle: Eigenvalues, Diagonalization and Linear Spaces
exam.instructions: Complete all tasks. Show complete solution approach for all calculations. Permitted aids: calculator without programming function. Good luck!

exercises.title: Gaussian elimination with free variables
exercises.description: Determine the solution set of $x_1 + x_2 + x_3 + x_4 = 4$, $x_1 + 2x_2 + 3x_3 + 4x_4 = 10$ in the form “particular solution $+$ solutions of the homogeneous system”.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Eliminate
$R_2 \to R_2 - R_1$: $x_2 + 2x_3 + 3x_4 = 6$. Rank $2$, four unknowns, so $4 - 2 = 2$ free variables: $x_3 = s$, $x_4 = t$.

Step 2: Back substitution
$x_2 = 6 - 2s - 3t$, $x_1 = 4 - x_2 - s - t = -2 + s + 2t$.

Step 3: Solution set
$L = \left\{(-2,6,0,0)^T + s(1,-2,1,0)^T + t(2,-3,0,1)^T \mid s,t \in \mathbb{R}\right\}$.

Step 4: Checks
Particular solution: $-2 + 6 = 4$ ✓, $-2 + 12 = 10$ ✓. Direction $(1,-2,1,0)$ in the homogeneous system: $1 - 2 + 1 = 0$ ✓, $1 - 4 + 3 = 0$ ✓. Direction $(2,-3,0,1)$: $2 - 3 + 1 = 0$ ✓, $2 - 6 + 4 = 0$ ✓.

exercises.title: Orthogonal diagonalisation
exercises.description:
Let $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$.
a) Determine the eigenvalues and an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors.
b) Give $Q$ with $Q^TAQ = D$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Eigenvalues
$\det(A - \lambda I) = (2-\lambda)\big((3-\lambda)^2 - 1\big) = (2-\lambda)(\lambda-2)(\lambda-4)$. Eigenvalues: $\lambda = 2$ (double), $\lambda = 4$.

Step 2: Part a): Eigenspaces
$\lambda = 2$: $v_2 + v_3 = 0$, $v_1$ free: $(1,0,0)$ and $(0,1,-1)$ (already orthogonal). $\lambda = 4$: $v_1 = 0$, $v_2 = v_3$: $(0,1,1)$.

Step 3: Part a): Normalise
$\vec q_1 = (1,0,0)$, $\vec q_2 = \frac1{\sqrt2}(0,1,-1)$, $\vec q_3 = \frac1{\sqrt2}(0,1,1)$. Orthogonality: $\vec q_2\cdot\vec q_3 = \frac12(1 - 1) = 0$ ✓ (eigenvectors for different eigenvalues of symmetric matrices are orthogonal).

Step 4: Part b): Matrix Q
$Q = (\vec q_1\,|\,\vec q_2\,|\,\vec q_3)$, $D = \operatorname{diag}(2,2,4)$ and $Q^TAQ = D$ since $Q^{-1} = Q^T$. Check: $\operatorname{tr}A = 8 = 2 + 2 + 4$ ✓, $\det A = 2\cdot8 = 16 = 2\cdot2\cdot4$ ✓.

exercises.title: Algebraic and geometric multiplicity
exercises.description: For which $a \in \mathbb{R}$ is $A_a = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & a \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ diagonalisable? Additionally determine whether $B = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ is diagonalisable.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Eigenvalues of A_a
Upper triangular matrix: eigenvalue $\lambda = 1$ with algebraic multiplicity $2$.

Step 2: Eigenspace of A_a
$A_a - I = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & a \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$. For $a = 0$: rank $0$, eigenspace $= \mathbb{R}^2$ (dimension $2$): diagonalisable ($A_0 = I$). For $a \neq 0$: rank $1$, eigenspace $\operatorname{span}\{(1,0)\}$ (dimension $1 < 2$): **not** diagonalisable.

Step 3: Matrix B
Eigenvalues $2$ (algebraic $2$) and $3$ (simple). $B - 2I = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ has rank $2$, hence eigenspace dimension $3 - 2 = 1 < 2$: $B$ is not diagonalisable.

Step 4: Remember
Diagonalisable $\iff$ for every eigenvalue algebraic and geometric multiplicity agree. Equal eigenvalues do not mean equal behaviour: $A_0$ and $A_1$ both have only the eigenvalue $1$.

exercises.title: Coordinates and representation matrix
exercises.description:
Let $B = \{\vec b_1,\vec b_2\} = \{(1,1),(1,-1)\}$ and $f(x,y) = (2x + y,\ x + 2y)$.
a) Determine the $B$-coordinates of $\vec v = (3,1)$.
b) Determine $[f]_B$ and interpret the result.
solutionSteps:
Step 2: Part b): Images of the basis vectors
$f(1,1) = (3,3) = 3\vec b_1 + 0\vec b_2$ and $f(1,-1) = (1,-1) = 0\vec b_1 + 1\vec b_2$.

Step 3: Part b): Matrix
$[f]_B = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ is diagonal.

Step 4: Interpretation and check
The basis vectors are eigenvectors for the eigenvalues $3$ and $1$. Check with the formula $[f]_B = T^{-1}AT$ with $T = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$: $[f]_B[\vec v]_B = (6,1)^T$, so $f(\vec v) = 6\vec b_1 + 1\vec b_2 = (7,5)$; directly $f(3,1) = (7,5)$ ✓.

exercises.title: Distance to a plane
exercises.description:
Let $U = \operatorname{span}\{(1,0,1),(0,1,1)\}$ and $\vec b = (1,1,1)$.
a) Determine a normal vector of $U$.
b) Determine the orthogonal projection of $\vec b$ onto $U$ and the distance from $\vec b$ to $U$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Normal vector
$\vec n$ must be perpendicular to both generators: $n_1 + n_3 = 0$ and $n_2 + n_3 = 0$. With $n_3 = -1$: $\vec n = (1,1,-1)$. (Alternatively cross product $(1,0,1)\times(0,1,1) = (-1,-1,1)$.)

Step 2: Part b): Projection
The component of $\vec b$ in the direction $\vec n$ is $\frac{\vec b\cdot\vec n}{\vec n\cdot\vec n}\vec n = \frac{1}{3}(1,1,-1)$. Projection onto $U$: $P\vec b = \vec b - \frac13\vec n = \left(\frac23,\frac23,\frac43\right)$.

Step 3: Part b): Distance
$d = \frac{|\vec b\cdot\vec n|}{|\vec n|} = \frac{1}{\sqrt3} \approx 0.577$.

Step 4: Check
$P\vec b \in U$: $\frac23(1,0,1) + \frac23(0,1,1) = \left(\frac23,\frac23,\frac43\right)$ ✓. The remainder $\frac13(1,1,-1)$ is parallel to $\vec n$, hence perpendicular to $U$ ✓.

exercises.title: Definiteness and principal axes
exercises.description:
Let $Q(x,y) = 2x^2 + 2xy + 2y^2$.
a) Determine the associated symmetric matrix and its eigenvalues.
b) Decide on the definiteness.
c) Describe the curve $Q(x,y) = 1$ (principal axes and semi-axes).
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Matrix and eigenvalues
$Q(\vec x) = \vec x^TA\vec x$ with $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ (the mixed coefficient $2$ is split as $1 + 1$). $\lambda^2 - 4\lambda + 3 = 0$: $\lambda_1 = 3$, $\lambda_2 = 1$.

Step 2: Part b): Definiteness
Both eigenvalues are positive: $Q$ is **positive definite**. Principal minors: $2 > 0$ and $\det A = 3 > 0$ ✓. Directly: $Q = x^2 + y^2 + (x+y)^2 > 0$ for $(x,y) \neq \vec0$.

Step 3: Part c): Principal axes
Eigenvectors: $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,1)$ for $3$ and $\frac1{\sqrt2}(1,-1)$ for $1$. In the new coordinates $u,v$ we have $Q = 3u^2 + v^2 = 1$.

Step 4: Part c): Semi-axes
Ellipse with semi-axes $\frac{1}{\sqrt3} \approx 0.577$ (in direction $(1,1)$) and $1$ (in direction $(1,-1)$). Check: $Q(1,-1) = 2 - 2 + 2 = 2$, so $Q\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,-1)\right) = 1$ ✓.
